I’m slowly coming around to the idea that if it works, I’m good with that. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job.
That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. To say this code is tested is … masterful understatement.
I think what helps is a long planning session, going into details, working out corner cases, designing test-cases, you know work and effort. Once that’s done it’s easier to let it work through the night and do a major production feature.
I still review the code, but hand on heart I couldn’t say I’d reviewed everything, sometimes I miss something in a complicated check-in. I try to keep checkins small and contained, but sometimes that’s not easy to manage alongside the “don’t break stuff” rule as well.
So it comes down to: I’ve been working on this for 6 months or so, and so far this has worked out for me. You know, kind of like getting used to a colleague’s idiosyncrasies over a period of time.
I will say that in my experience the code quality is fairly high. Maybe that’s down to the effort put in ahead of time in the planning stages, I don’t know, but I don’t seem to suffer from the ‘slop’ that people complain of. YMMV.

The original EPCOT as imagined by Walt Disney was a master-planned city, with all the pleasant amenities and cleverest design you could imagine in the 1960's: Walkable areas, clean public transit, no traffic congestion, homes furnished with the latest in technology and appliances. It was his greatest ambition at the end of his life to make it a reality.
But it didn't happen. Namely, because of how much central control would be given to one man and/or his company to pull it off. The plan in its early iterations essentially meant that if you lived in EPCOT, you forfeited certain freedoms, such as what goes in your home, where you worked, and so on.
This game gave me a good chuckle as a Sim City fan. I'm guilty of complaining about politicians of all levels. But I don't envy their position of having to cut through the vines of competing motives and regulations. And at the same time, as a citizen, I'm not sure I would opt for the Utopian alternative.

text:
+1. I personally have always wanted to write down my thoughts on NixOS in a long-ish form post.
But it’s just really hard to articulate. NixOS is such a step above any other distro that it becomes hard to convey exactly why this is the case. It is also because so many pieces work together in tandem - both above and below the covers so to speak - to make this the case.
There is really only one talk I have found that captures this, it is What Nix Can Do (and Can’t) by Matthew Croughan: https://youtu.be/6Le0IbPRzOE
Also, here is a random dump of features that I have found both valuable and very difficult to achieve on other distros:
* Config rollback in bootloader to undo mistakes without needing to boot from recovery media
* Flake lockfiles to pin all config and packages
* Config layering: base config that applies to all machines, per-machine overrides, etc
* NixOS module system, very useful to conditionally enable functionality (e.g. subset of machines run Syncthing)
* Rebuild a host over SSH by copying over packages via nixos-rebuild
* Image builders i.e. Packer-lite (now in nixpkgs)
* Build a live CD/USB custom installer to quickly boot from with your own packages, user, dotfiles, etc
* NixOS integration testing framework (extremely powerful), makes package and config stability better under the hood in nixpkgs
* Build and run your config as a QEMU VM
* nixos-anywhere to convert a running Linux machine into NixOS, very useful for VPS/cloud machines
* Out of the box support for cross compilation and static linking via pkgsCross and pkgsStatic
* Stylix for centralized theming config across apps
* Natively build a Docker image from your package using dockerTools

One thing you can try is to build specialised subagents to help tease out more thinking when you're stuck with a model with limited reasoning budget as all the codex sub models seem to be (compared to API) --- but I have no firm, hard evidence of this so treat it as guesswork on my part.
Let me explain.
Creat a subagent that is told to just mull about a subject. This can be a simple file.
Have the agent expound on it with its own thoughts and additions.
Now rinse and repeat: give the file to another blank 'reasoning' subagent; then another; and so on.
This will eventually reach a point where they are unlikely to add more real value.
I believe they've locked down temperature and other sampling parameters so you cannot tweak these to get it to consider more unusual approaches.
The absolute best approach is a second model that is of a different family. Try Deepseek, GLM, Qwen, etc. and have it add its own thoughts. As a bonus, these models do not hide their reasoning. Put that in a file also.

After consuming my whole usage window in a few minutes multiple times, I realised I needed  a hook to do some checks for me and prompt me before submitting when cache had expired and content is too big, so that it can suggest me to "compact then send". It can also prevent sub-agents from spawning when above 80% usage window. Control is handed over to the user.
The first I built, based on hooks (run for 75 days), the biggest burst fell from 365 agent spawned to 27, and requests over 500k tokens of context from 14.5% to 0.6%. Lockouts still went up, because lots of parallel main sessions use up the window too. The strength is that it counts agents across every session on the machine.
I built https://github.com/rbartoli/agent-usage-guard, MIT-licensed, makes no network calls, needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later.
I have also a post on this:  https://rblab.com/what-stops-claude-code-burning-your-usage-window/

text:
Hi HN,
I'm obsessive about my phone, and those who are paying the bill are my two babies. When I get off work, I spend time with them, but the phone is glued to my hand. I'll catch myself looking up and I haven't been connecting with them at all. I'm getting better.
So I experimented with everything, including what all the usual advice on reddit says:
- Screen Time with passcode. This worked for several days. But I created the passcode so I knew it and I just typed in the passcode and unlocked. Nearly all of the iPhone blocker apps are built on top of Screen Time so they suffer the same problem. Screen Time can also be circumvented by a few tricks that I won't go into here.
- Handing over your passcode to a friend. Works, but sometimes I actually do need an app, say a web browser, and I can't keep bothering someone every time I need it locked or unlocked.
- A physical time-lock box. Yeah, this one actually does work, and I would recommend it. Just not if you need your phone - authenticator, phone calls, alarm, maps, banking apps, mobile wallet.
Next I discovered Assistive Access, which is built into iOS and substitutes the home screen with just the apps you select. Believe me, you'll end up so bored by your phone you won't want to use it. However, this method has the same flaw: it has its own passcode, and if you know it, you can get out of it.
But Assistive Access is cruel in one respect. When you create the passcode, it offers to add a recovery Apple Account. If you pass on that, and you don't remember the passcode, there is no freakin way out. Your only escape hatch is erasing your phone and restoring everything, and you do not want to do that.
So the fix: don't know the passcode.
Honestly, you don't need my app for this. Let a friend or your partner set the Assistive Access passcode for you, skip the recovery account, and you're done. If that works for you, great.
I wanted to get this done myself every time, on demand, without relying on someone. However you do it I am sure you will like it. This is the only thing that has worked for me and I am reclaiming my evenings.
That's what Screen Fasting does:
1. Select the duration of your fast.
2. We create a 4 digit passcode, you type it in as a 14-15 digit sequence with fake outs and deletes. Once setup is complete, you can't remember what you actually typed.
3. Until the time you selected runs out, there is no way back. When it does, we send you the passcode by email.
So don't just click everything when selecting your allowed apps. Leave Phone, Messages and any others you'll need if anything happens.
For iPhone/iPad only, iOS 17+ We have to keep the passcode so we can send it back to you when your fast ends.
Note: this is just the Assistive Access passcode, not the passcode on your iPhone or Apple ID password. It is only an Assistive Access specific passcode, which means it cannot be used to unlock your phone or access your data.
Any feedback for me, particularly in the setup flow: where did you get stuck & wanted to quit?

I have been building something similar except not for Minecraft but hiking maps on mobile (Android). This is my app: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.chessvortexgames.maps
I combine OpenStreetMap data for routes, satellite data from Sentinel-2 and Copernicus DEM GLO-30 for heights, resolution is around 10m/pixel for image and 30m for heights - those are the highest resolution datasets I can legally redistribute, although I am also including what I call hi-res maps building for some countries (USA, France, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Romania) which has image resolution at 1.5m/pixel instead of 10m.
I could have used higher resolution for hi-res maps, data is available at precision like 30-50cm/pixel but this being a mobile app I needed to consider storage for a map on mobile, at hi-res a 10x10 km squared area takes around 25MB.
The idea for this came from my own hiking trips, in many mountains there is not so good internet connection, so I can build an offline map beforehand and in terrain I can use this to see where I am in 3D - and just use the phone GPS for location, no data needed.
For building the map packages I have setup a linux server that combines all 3 data sources (OpenStreetMap, Sentinel-2, Copernicus GLO-30) so once an area is chosen it can build it in like 1-3 minutes. Since all OSM endpoints are giving lots of timeouts I setup a local OSM mirror with the data that I need - takes around 50GB of storage for the whole world data and I have a script that updates it weekly.
Coming back to the original post, seeing 1:1 ratio of Switzerland made my heart stop for a bit, then I realized it's 1m resolution. Switzerland was also my first choice for hi-res data, they provide good accurate image and height datasets. Pretty cool all this Minecraft voxel rendering, I intend to see how it would look in my own app.

I'm working on "Cargo but for C".
It started out as something marginally more useful than vendoring your dependencies as submodules + baking in the knowledge of how to build a bunch of common projects.
I realized, though, that there was somehow a huge gap in the insane world of C build tools. There's nothing that:
- Lets you pin really precisely and builds everything from source (i.e. no binary repository)
- Does not depend on either a scripting language or a completely insane DSL (Conan uses Python, CMake is an eldritch horror, ditto Make, lots of other tools of course but none of them quite hit the mark)
- Has a good balance of "builds are data" and "builds are code".
Anyway, it's going great. There are, of course, a ton of problems to solve. Chief among them is the obvious caveat that C is not a monoculture like Rust. There will be zero upstream libraries that use this tool natively. But I don't think it matters. I think I can build something which is as much better to the existing tools as, say, UV was to existing Python tools, even with that disadvantage.

https://mytinycafe.com/
An PWA primarily for my wife and my daughter. They can order their hot chocolate and their coffee as if they were going to grab something at a fancy café downtown, but instead it's at home and I'm the barista. It is quite nice to have for when my wife comes back from work and want something specific, or when we are waiting for the visit of a few friend, they can order exactly the available beverages and everything is ready when they're here.
It was also a good playground for me to implement Web Push notifications (to never miss new orders).
It's a basic Nuxt 3 app with Appwrite as the backend with rough edges, but much enough for our household use !
If you want to spam my phone with notifications, please visit my café : https://mytinycafe.com/alix
